task_row_model.query: How can I implement atomic increments of a shared integer counter across multiple Python processes on Unix and Windows using multiprocessing or shared_memory?

documents.content: In CPython's multiprocessing library the synchronized wrapper multiprocessing.Value(typecode, initial) creates a shared ctypes object with an internal lock. Code typically acquires the lock via value.get_lock() or by using a with value.get_lock(): block before mutating the .value attribute to ensure atomic updates across processes. multiprocessing.RawValue(typecode, initial) provides the same shared memory layout but does not create or manage a lock, so concurrent increments on a RawValue are racy unless an external Lock is used. Note: when using the spawn start method (the default on Windows) child processes are initialized by pickling the objects passed to them; therefore synchronization objects should be created in the main process and passed into each worker. Boilerplate examples often show if __name__ == '__main__': guards for program entry on spawn systems.

The multiprocessing.shared_memory module (introduced in recent Python releases) exposes SharedMemory and ShareableList for raw shared buffers; these primitives do not include synchronization or atomic operations. Journalistic guides recommend combining shared_memory with synchronization primitives from multiprocessing: either create a multiprocessing.Lock and use it to protect increments, or use a multiprocessing.Manager() to host a proxy Value which is picklable and operates across spawn-based starts. Managers give a higher-level proxy object that serializes requests through a server process, which avoids some pickling pitfalls. Practical advice: on Windows (spawn) you must create locks/Manager objects in main and pass references into subprocesses; on Unix, fork-based starts inherit memory, but you still must synchronize access to shared state to avoid races.

Note from an engineer: Raw shared memory (sharedctypes or shared_memory) is fast but bare — no atomic increment primitive is provided. You can either: (1) use multiprocessing.Value with its built-in lock and call get_lock(), or (2) allocate a SharedMemory buffer and serialize updates through a multiprocessing.Lock created in main. On Unix the fork start will copy file descriptors and can inherit locks; this historical behavior differs from Windows spawn, which re-imports the module and reinitializes state, making the if __name__ == '__main__' guard essential. As an aside, people often conflate the GIL (thread-level) with process synchronization; the GIL does not protect across processes. Some blog posts repeat the same cautions and anecdotal benchmarks about RawValue being slightly faster than Value because of locking overhead.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Create a multiprocessing.Value('i', 0) or a Manager().Value and perform increments while holding its lock (use value.get_lock() or an explicit multiprocessing.Lock). RawValue or shared_memory buffers provide no synchronization, so protect them with a multiprocessing.Lock. On spawn-based starts (Windows) create the Value/Lock (or Manager) in if __name__ == '__main__' and pass them to workers; on Unix fork you still must use these locks to avoid races.
